# Descriptive Statistics and Figures **Week 3**: Summarising data and producing figures with ggplot2 Before testing any hypothesis, you need to describe your data: where the centre is, how spread out the values are, and what the data look like. In this workshop you will learn which summary statistics suit which kinds of data, and how to build clear, publication-quality figures with `ggplot2`. Workshop materials are available in the GitHub repository [ECS200](https://github.com/nicholaswunz/ECS200-Workshop). ![](images/base_visual.png) ::: {.callout-tip} ## Learning outcomes By the end of this workshop you should be able to: 1. Choose suitable measures of centre and spread for different types of variables. 2. Explain the difference between a standard deviation, a standard error and a confidence interval. 3. Calculate summary statistics for groups with `group_by()` and `summarise()`. 4. Build histograms, boxplots, dot plots and scatterplots with `ggplot2`, and polish them for a report. ::: ## Background {.unnumbered} The right summary depends on the **scale** of the variable: | Scale | Type | Definition | Examples | Centre | Spread | |:------|:-----|:-----------|:---------|:-------|:-------| | Nominal | Categorical | Named categories with no order | Sex, species, habitat | Mode | Counts, proportions | | Ordinal | Categorical | Categories with a natural order | Life stage (egg, juvenile, adult), damage score 0–5 | Median, mode | Range, IQR | | Interval | Numeric | Equal intervals, no true zero | Temperature (°C), pH, dates | Mean, median | SD, SE, CI | | Ratio | Numeric | Equal intervals and a true zero | Length, mass, age, counts | Mean, median | SD, SE, CV, IQR, CI | When you design a data sheet, think about what type each column will be. Here is an example colour-coded by type: [nominal]{style="background-color: #fadbfa;"}, [continuous]{style="background-color: #cce8ff;"}, [ordinal]{style="background-color: #fff2c0;"} and [binary]{style="background-color: #c6fbf5;"}. ![](images/types-of-variables.png){width=100%} Key terms used in this workshop. Central tendancy: - **Mean**: the average. Best for roughly symmetrical data. - **Median**: the middle value. Robust to outliers and skew. - **Mode**: the most frequent value (useful for categories). Spread: - **Standard deviation (SD)**: how spread out the **data** are around the mean. - **Standard error (SE)**: SD / √*n*. How precisely the **mean** has been estimated. - **95% confidence interval (CI)**: a range that is likely to contain the true mean (mean ± about 2 × SE). - **Coefficient of variation (CV)**: SD / mean. Compares variability between variables measured on different scales. - **Interquartile range (IQR)**: the range of the middle 50% of the data (Q3 − Q1). - **Variance**: SD². The average squared distance from the mean. CrashCourse Statistics has short videos on [measures of central tendency](https://youtu.be/kn83BA7cRNM?si=qzoPZk44hZRlzo9P) and [measures of spread](https://youtu.be/R4yfNi_8Kqw?si=9QO_QzRmLG5oyQjH) if you would like a refresher. # Before we start {.unnumbered} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Week 3 workshop - Descriptive statistics # Written by Nicholas Wu, 1234578, 11/03/2027 # install.packages("patchwork") # run once in the console if needed library(tidyverse) # data wrangling and ggplot2 library(patchwork) # combine several ggplots into one figure # setwd("C:/Users/YOUR-NAME/Documents/ECS200") ``` ::: # Part 1: Descriptive statistics {.unnumbered} ::: {.panel-tabset .nav-pills} ## Centre {.unnumbered} Whether to use the mean or the median depends on the shape of the distribution. In skewed data, a few extreme values pull the mean towards the long tail, while the median stays in the middle. ![](images/mean_mod_median.png){width=85%} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Simulate a symmetrical (normal) and a right-skewed variable, 100 values each set.seed(1) # makes the random numbers the same every time dist_data <- data.frame(normal = rnorm(100, mean = 10, sd = 2), skewed = rexp(100, rate = 0.2)) dist_data %>% dplyr::summarise(normal_mean = mean(normal), normal_median = median(normal), skewed_mean = mean(skewed), skewed_median = median(skewed)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` normal_mean normal_median skewed_mean skewed_median 1 10.21777 10.22782 4.656321 3.781882 ``` ::: ::: For the normal data the mean and median are almost the same (about 10). For the skewed data the mean (about 4.7) is much larger than the median (about 3). ## Spread {.unnumbered} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dist_data %>% dplyr::summarise(n = dplyr::n(), mean = mean(skewed), variance = var(skewed), sd = sd(skewed), # standard deviation se = sd / sqrt(n), # standard error ci_lower = mean - qt(0.975, df = n - 1) * se, # lower 95% confidence limit ci_upper = mean + qt(0.975, df = n - 1) * se, # upper 95% confidence limit cv = sd / mean) # coefficient of variation ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` n mean variance sd se ci_lower ci_upper cv 1 100 4.656321 13.85892 3.722757 0.3722757 3.917645 5.394997 0.799506 ``` ::: ::: `qt(0.975, df = n - 1)` is the number of standard errors needed for a 95% CI. It is close to 2 for large samples and gets bigger for small samples. - The **SD** describes the spread of the **data**, and does not shrink as you collect more data. - The **SE** and **CI** describe the uncertainty in the **mean**, and get smaller as the sample size grows. The SD and CI assume the data are roughly symmetrical, so for skewed data a boxplot (median and quartiles) is often a better summary. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Long format: one column says which distribution, one column holds the value dist_long <- dist_data %>% tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "data_type", values_to = "value") dist_stats <- dist_long %>% dplyr::group_by(data_type) %>% dplyr::summarise(mean = mean(value), sd = sd(value)) # Histograms with the mean (solid) and mean +/- 1 SD (dashed) ggplot2::ggplot(dist_long, ggplot2::aes(x = value)) + ggplot2::geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "grey80") + ggplot2::geom_vline(data = dist_stats, ggplot2::aes(xintercept = mean), linewidth = 1) + ggplot2::geom_vline(data = dist_stats, ggplot2::aes(xintercept = mean - sd), linetype = "dashed") + ggplot2::geom_vline(data = dist_stats, ggplot2::aes(xintercept = mean + sd), linetype = "dashed") + ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ data_type, scales = "free") + ggplot2::labs(x = "Value", y = "Frequency", subtitle = "Mean ± SD: for skewed data, mean − SD can even fall below zero") + ggplot2::theme_classic() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week03_descriptive_stats_files/figure-html/spread-plot-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: ## Quantiles {.unnumbered} Quantiles split sorted data into equal parts. The quartiles (25%, 50% and 75%) are what a boxplot shows. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Min, quartiles and max with base R quantile(dist_data$skewed) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 0% 25% 50% 75% 100% 0.1012521 1.7143874 3.7818821 7.1284592 16.2966855 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # The same with dplyr (this also works with group_by()) dist_data %>% dplyr::summarise(min = min(skewed), q1 = quantile(skewed, probs = 0.25), median = median(skewed), q3 = quantile(skewed, probs = 0.75), max = max(skewed), iqr = IQR(skewed)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` min q1 median q3 max iqr 1 0.1012521 1.714387 3.781882 7.128459 16.29669 5.414072 ``` ::: ::: ::: The app below shows why it matters whether you plot the SD, SE or CI. Increase the sample size and see what happens to each. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## What happens, and why? (try the app first, then open this) The three error bars answer **different questions**: | | Formula | Question it answers | When *n* increases | When the true SD increases | |:--|:--|:--|:--|:--| | **SD** | $\sqrt{\frac{\sum(x - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}}$ | How much do individual measurements vary? | Stays about the same | Gets wider | | **SE** | $\frac{SD}{\sqrt{n}}$ | How precisely do we know the mean? | Shrinks | Gets wider | | **95% CI** | $\bar{x} \pm t \times SE$ | Where is the true population mean likely to be? | Shrinks, fastest at small *n* | Gets wider | **Increasing the sample size** - **SD stays about the same.** The SD describes the spread of the population, and that does not change because you measured more individuals. With a larger sample, your estimate of the SD just gets closer to the true value (it jumps around less when you press *Resample*). - **SE shrinks.** The SE divides the SD by $\sqrt{n}$. More data gives a more precise estimate of the mean, but with diminishing returns: to halve the SE you need **four times** as many samples (e.g. from 10 to 40). - **The CI shrinks even faster at small *n*.** The CI is the SE multiplied by a value from the *t* distribution. With very few samples, *t* is large (4.3 when *n* = 3) because we are unsure about the SD as well as the mean. As *n* grows, *t* drops towards about 2 (2.26 at *n* = 10, 1.98 at *n* = 100), so the 95% CI ends up at roughly **2 × SE**. **Increasing the true SD** - **All three get wider in proportion.** If individuals vary more, the data are more spread out (larger SD), and the mean is harder to pin down (larger SE and CI). Doubling the SD doubles all three bars. - The y-axis of the app rescales with the SD, so the bars may *look* similar. Read the numbers under the plot. **Why it matters** - Use the **SD** when you want to show how variable the organisms or sites are (e.g. "lizards weighed 15.2 ± 2.1 g, mean ± SD"). - Use the **SE** or **95% CI** when you want to show how precisely you have estimated the mean, or to compare groups. The CI is the easier one to interpret. - A small SE does not mean the data have little variation; it may just mean a large sample. This is why you must **always state which one your error bars show**. ::: ::: {.app-box .column-body-outset} ::: {.app-title} App: standard deviation, standard error and confidence interval ::: ```{ojs} //| echo: false //| output: false import {rng, rnorm, mean, sd, qt975, fmt, red, grey, dark, blue} from "./apps/ecs200.js" ``` ::: {.app-grid} ::: {.app-controls} ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof ds_n = Inputs.range([3, 200], {value: 10, step: 1, label: "Sample size (n)"}) viewof ds_sd = Inputs.range([0.5, 5], {value: 2, step: 0.1, label: "True SD of the population"}) viewof ds_seed = Inputs.button("Resample") ``` ::: ::: {.app-output} ```{ojs} //| echo: false ds_data = { const r = rng(33 + ds_seed); const x = rnorm(r, ds_n, 20, ds_sd); const m = mean(x), s = sd(x), se = s / Math.sqrt(ds_n), ci = qt975(ds_n - 1) * se; const pts = x.map((v) => ({x: 1 + (r() - 0.5) * 0.5, y: v})); const bars = [ {x: 2.2, lo: m - s, hi: m + s, lab: "Mean ± SD"}, {x: 3.0, lo: m - se, hi: m + se, lab: "Mean ± SE"}, {x: 3.8, lo: m - ci, hi: m + ci, lab: "Mean ± 95% CI"} ]; return {pts, bars, m, s, se, ci}; } html`
${Plot.plot({ width: 560, height: 300, marginLeft: 45, x: {domain: [0.5, 4.3], ticks: [1, 2.2, 3.0, 3.8], tickFormat: (d) => ({1: "Raw data", 2.2: "± SD", 3: "± SE", 3.8: "± 95% CI"})[d], label: null}, y: {label: "Measurement", grid: true, domain: [20 - 3.5 * ds_sd, 20 + 3.5 * ds_sd]}, marks: [ Plot.dot(ds_data.pts, {x: "x", y: "y", fill: grey, fillOpacity: 0.5, r: 2.5}), Plot.ruleX(ds_data.bars, {x: "x", y1: "lo", y2: "hi", stroke: red, strokeWidth: 3}), Plot.dot(ds_data.bars, {x: "x", y: () => ds_data.m, fill: red, r: 5}) ] })}
Mean = ${fmt(ds_data.m)}, SD = ${fmt(ds_data.s)}, SE = ${fmt(ds_data.se)}, 95% CI half-width = ${fmt(ds_data.ci)}. The SD stays about the same as n grows (it describes the data), while the SE and CI shrink (they describe how precisely we know the mean). Always say which one your error bars show.
` ``` ::: ::: ::: ### Exercise 1 (5 min) {.unnumbered} 🧪 **Summarise species 3 in this survey** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey_data <- data.frame( site = c("A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B", "C", "C", "C"), plot = c(1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3), species_1 = c(12, 7, 15, 4, 9, 6, 20, 18, 25), species_2 = c(5, 2, 1, 10, 7, 4, 3, 1, 0), species_3 = c(0, 3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 0, 1, 2), species_4 = c(8, 6, 3, 1, 4, 2, 10, 7, 5) ) ``` ::: - Calculate the mean, standard deviation and sample size of `species_3`. - Does a mean make sense for count data like these? What else could you report?
Show answer ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey_data %>% dplyr::summarise(mean = mean(species_3), sd = sd(species_3), median = median(species_3), n = dplyr::n()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mean sd median n 1 2.555556 2.127858 2 9 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # mean = 2.56, SD = 2.13, n = 9. A mean of 2.56 individuals is not a possible # count, but it is still a valid average. The median (2) and range (0 to 6) # are also useful for small counts. ``` :::
## By groups {.unnumbered} Most of the time you want summaries for each group, e.g. each site, species or treatment. Convert the data to long format, then use `group_by()`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey_long <- survey_data %>% tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = species_1:species_4, names_to = "species", values_to = "abundance") # Mean, SD and sample size of abundance for each site and species survey_summary <- survey_long %>% dplyr::group_by(site, species) %>% dplyr::summarise(mean = mean(abundance), sd = sd(abundance), n = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop") # remove the grouping afterwards survey_summary ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 12 × 5 site species mean sd n 1 A species_1 11.3 4.04 3 2 A species_2 2.67 2.08 3 3 A species_3 1.67 1.53 3 4 A species_4 5.67 2.52 3 5 B species_1 6.33 2.52 3 6 B species_2 7 3 3 7 B species_3 5 1 3 8 B species_4 2.33 1.53 3 9 C species_1 21 3.61 3 10 C species_2 1.33 1.53 3 11 C species_3 1 1 3 12 C species_4 7.33 2.52 3 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Mean +/- SD for each species at each site ggplot2::ggplot(survey_summary, ggplot2::aes(x = site, y = mean, ymin = mean - sd, ymax = mean + sd, colour = species)) + ggplot2::geom_pointrange(position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = 0.6)) + # dodge so species don't overlap ggplot2::labs(x = "Site", y = "Abundance (mean ± SD)", colour = "Species") + ggplot2::theme_classic() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week03_descriptive_stats_files/figure-html/groups-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: # Part 2: Figures with ggplot2 {.unnumbered} The "gg" in `ggplot2` stands for *grammar of graphics*. You build a plot in **layers**, joined with `+`: 1. `ggplot2::ggplot(data, ggplot2::aes(x = ..., y = ...))` sets the data and which columns go on which axis (the *aesthetics*). 2. `geom_...()` layers draw the data: points, lines, boxes, bars. 3. `labs()`, `scale_...()`, `theme_...()` and `facet_...()` adjust labels, colours, the overall look and panels. ![](images/ggplot_layout.png){width=100%} Before plotting, decide which variable is the **independent** (predictor, on the *x*-axis) and which is the **dependent** (response, on the *y*-axis) variable. ![](images/independent-vs-dependent-variables.png){width=100%} ### Plot types {.unnumbered} Which plot to use depends on the types of variables you have: ![](images/DL_datavis1_which_plot.png){width=90%} We will use the clean sugar maple data from Weeks 1 and 2 to compare stem length between the calcium-treated (**W1**) and untreated (**Reference**) watersheds. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plant_data <- readr::read_csv("data/plant_calcium_task.csv") %>% dplyr::mutate(watershed = dplyr::if_else(watershed == "W2", "W1", watershed), watershed = factor(watershed), total_mass_mg = (leaf_dry_mass + stem_dry_mass) * 1000) %>% dplyr::filter(stem_dry_mass < 1) ``` ::: ::: {.panel-tabset .nav-pills} ## Histogram or density {.unnumbered} ![](images/histogram.png){width=90%} A [histogram](https://r-graph-gallery.com/histogram) cuts a numeric variable into bins and shows how many observations fall in each. A [density plot](https://r-graph-gallery.com/density-plot) is a smoothed version. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot2::ggplot(plant_data, ggplot2::aes(x = stem_length, fill = watershed)) + ggplot2::geom_histogram(alpha = 0.5, position = "identity", bins = 30) + # alpha makes overlapping bars see-through ggplot2::labs(x = "Stem length (mm)", y = "Count", fill = "Watershed") + ggplot2::theme_classic() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week03_descriptive_stats_files/figure-html/hist-1.png){width=768} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot2::ggplot(plant_data, ggplot2::aes(x = stem_length, fill = watershed)) + ggplot2::geom_density(alpha = 0.5) + ggplot2::labs(x = "Stem length (mm)", y = "Density", fill = "Watershed") + ggplot2::theme_classic() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week03_descriptive_stats_files/figure-html/hist-2.png){width=768} ::: ::: ## Boxplot {.unnumbered} ![](images/boxplot.png){width=90%} A [boxplot](https://r-graph-gallery.com/89-box-and-scatter-plot-with-ggplot2.html) summarises a numeric variable: - the thick **line** is the median; - the **box** spans the lower (Q1) and upper (Q3) quartiles, so it contains the middle 50% of the data (the IQR); - the **whiskers** extend to the most extreme values within 1.5 × IQR of the box; - **points** beyond the whiskers are potential outliers. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot2::ggplot(plant_data, ggplot2::aes(x = watershed, y = stem_length)) + ggplot2::geom_boxplot() + ggplot2::labs(x = "Watershed", y = "Stem length (mm)") + ggplot2::theme_classic() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week03_descriptive_stats_files/figure-html/boxplot-1.png){width=480} ::: ::: ## Bar plot or dot plot {.unnumbered} ![](images/bar-plot.png){width=90%} Bar plots of means hide the data, so a **dot plot** of the mean ± SD (or SE or CI) over the raw data is usually a better choice. You need a summary table and the raw data, so each layer gets its own `data =`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plant_summary <- plant_data %>% dplyr::group_by(watershed) %>% dplyr::summarise(mean = mean(stem_length), sd = sd(stem_length)) # Bar plot of the mean +/- SD bar_plot <- ggplot2::ggplot(plant_summary, ggplot2::aes(x = watershed, y = mean)) + ggplot2::geom_col(fill = "grey70") + ggplot2::geom_errorbar(ggplot2::aes(ymin = mean - sd, ymax = mean + sd), width = 0.1) + ggplot2::labs(x = "Watershed", y = "Stem length (mm)", title = "Bar plot") + ggplot2::theme_classic() # Raw data with the mean +/- SD on top dot_plot <- ggplot2::ggplot() + ggplot2::geom_jitter(data = plant_data, ggplot2::aes(x = watershed, y = stem_length), width = 0.15, alpha = 0.2) + ggplot2::geom_pointrange(data = plant_summary, ggplot2::aes(x = watershed, y = mean, ymin = mean - sd, ymax = mean + sd), colour = "#e12744") + ggplot2::labs(x = "Watershed", y = "Stem length (mm)", title = "Dot plot with raw data") + ggplot2::theme_classic() # patchwork: put two plots side by side with + bar_plot + dot_plot ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week03_descriptive_stats_files/figure-html/dot-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: ## Scatterplot {.unnumbered} ![](images/scatter-plot.png){width=90%} A [scatterplot](https://r-graph-gallery.com/scatterplot) shows the relationship between two numeric variables. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot2::ggplot(plant_data, ggplot2::aes(x = stem_length, y = stem_dry_mass, colour = watershed)) + ggplot2::geom_point() + ggplot2::labs(x = "Stem length (mm)", y = "Stem dry mass (g)", colour = "Watershed") + ggplot2::theme_classic() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week03_descriptive_stats_files/figure-html/scatter-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: ::: ### Polishing plots {.unnumbered} ::: {.panel-tabset .nav-pills} ## Themes {.unnumbered} Themes change the overall look in one line, e.g. `theme_classic()`, `theme_bw()` or `theme_minimal()`. ![](images/visualization-themes.png){width=100%} ## Labels {.unnumbered} Always give axes informative labels **with units**. `labs()` sets the axis, legend and title labels in one place. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot2::ggplot(plant_data, ggplot2::aes(x = watershed, y = stem_length)) + ggplot2::geom_boxplot() + ggplot2::labs(title = "Your title", subtitle = "Your subtitle", x = "Treatment", # use x = NULL to remove a label y = "Stem length (mm)") + ggplot2::theme_classic() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week03_descriptive_stats_files/figure-html/labels-1.png){width=480} ::: ::: ## Shapes and sizes {.unnumbered} ![Point shapes and their numbers.](images/points-symbols.png){width=70%} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot2::ggplot(plant_data, ggplot2::aes(x = stem_length, y = stem_dry_mass, shape = watershed)) + ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2) + ggplot2::scale_shape_manual(values = c(1, 16)) + # open and filled circles ggplot2::labs(x = "Stem length (mm)", y = "Stem dry mass (g)", shape = "Watershed") + ggplot2::theme_classic() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week03_descriptive_stats_files/figure-html/shapes-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## Colours {.unnumbered} `colour` changes outlines, points and lines, and `fill` changes the inside of shapes. Set one colour for everything inside the `geom`, or map a variable inside `aes()` and choose the colours with `scale_colour_manual()` or `scale_fill_manual()`. You can use [R colour names](https://www.nceas.ucsb.edu/sites/default/files/2020-04/colorPaletteCheatsheet.pdf) (e.g. `"tomato"`) or hex codes (e.g. `"#e12744"`). Choose colours that are colour-blind friendly, such as those in the [`colorspace`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/colorspace/vignettes/colorspace.html) package. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # One fill colour for every box one_colour <- ggplot2::ggplot(plant_data, ggplot2::aes(x = watershed, y = stem_length)) + ggplot2::geom_boxplot(fill = "#F5C4B8") + ggplot2::labs(x = "Watershed", y = "Stem length (mm)", subtitle = "One colour") + ggplot2::theme_classic() # Fill colour by group group_colour <- ggplot2::ggplot(plant_data, ggplot2::aes(x = watershed, y = stem_length, fill = watershed)) + ggplot2::geom_boxplot() + ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = c("Reference" = "#B8CEF5", "W1" = "#F5C4B8")) + ggplot2::labs(x = "Watershed", y = "Stem length (mm)", fill = "Watershed", subtitle = "Colour by group") + ggplot2::theme_classic() one_colour + group_colour ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week03_descriptive_stats_files/figure-html/colours-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: A numeric variable mapped to colour gives a colour gradient: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot2::ggplot(plant_data, ggplot2::aes(x = stem_length, y = stem_dry_mass, colour = leaf_dry_mass)) + ggplot2::geom_point() + ggplot2::scale_colour_viridis_c() + # a colour-blind-friendly gradient ggplot2::labs(x = "Stem length (mm)", y = "Stem dry mass (g)", colour = "Leaf dry\nmass (g)") + ggplot2::theme_classic() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week03_descriptive_stats_files/figure-html/gradient-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## Panels (facets) {.unnumbered} `facet_wrap()` splits a plot into panels, one for each level of a variable. Decide which variable to put in panels and which to show with colour based on the comparison you want readers to make. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot2::ggplot(plant_data, ggplot2::aes(x = stem_length, y = stem_dry_mass, colour = watershed)) + ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.7) + ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c("Reference" = "grey40", "W1" = "#e12744")) + ggplot2::labs(x = "Stem length (mm)", y = "Stem dry mass (g)", colour = "Watershed") + ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ year) + # one panel per year ggplot2::theme_classic() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week03_descriptive_stats_files/figure-html/facets-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: ## Combining plots {.unnumbered} The `patchwork` package combines separate ggplots: `+` or `|` puts them side by side, and `/` stacks them. `plot_annotation()` adds panel letters. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} (one_colour + group_colour) / bar_plot + patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_levels = "a") # label panels a, b, c ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](week03_descriptive_stats_files/figure-html/patchwork-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: To save a figure for your report, use `ggplot2::ggsave("figures/fig1.png", width = 16, height = 10, units = "cm", dpi = 300)`. `width` is the width of the plot in cm, `height` is the height of the plot in cm, and `dpi` (dots per inch) is the resolution of the figure ::: # Assessment {.unnumbered} Task to complete before the end of the workshop.
